newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Infratil sees lower NZ electricity prices.
newsitem.headline: Infratil sees lower NZ electricity prices.

text.p: Infrastructure and Investments Ltd (Infratil) expects New Zealand wholesale electricity prices to fall in the short term, reducing investment returns, the company said in its March Update commentary.
"In the short term, Infratil expects excess generation capacity will put downward pressure on electricity prices, and investment returns," Infratil said.
Supply and demand were fairly well balanced in the current year, but Infratil said it may take another six years of load growth before new plant now coming on stream was absorbed.
"Hence, we are already seeing electricity contract prices tracking down in real terms," it said.
In the longer term, electricity prices would need to reflect the costs of bringing more power plants on stream.

But Infratil said the large scale plant that would determine long term electricity prices was likely to be gas fired, and noted the substantial falls in the per kilowatt costs of combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) plant over the last three years, as well as improvements in plant effiencies.

"These trends are expected to continue, albeit at a reduced rate," Infratil said, adding it anticipates a 2.0 percent per annum real fall in plant costs and a 0.5 percent per annum improvement in efficiency for CCGT over the next five years.

"Overall, declining plant costs and ongoing efficiency improvements will provide significant scope to absorb considerable increases in the cost of gas without any upward pressure on electricity prices," Infratil said.
"We see little reason for electricity prices to rise even after the current excess supply situation passses. If wholesale gas prices remain stable, electricity prices are likely to fall."

Infratil said its electricity generation investment strategy was therefore to look for specific niche market opportunities where regional transmission aspects, high loss factors or special fuel options improved investment economics.
